planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock directly beside cold, moving water or on a perpetually seep-fed rock face in fall; lettuce saxifrage will not tolerate ordinary garden soil moisture and needs essentially constant wetness at its roots.

directions: Lettuce saxifrage grows rooted directly in the splash zone of cold Southern Appalachian mountain streams and seepage rock faces, forming a rosette of large, light-green, spoon-shaped leaves that were historically gathered as an early-spring potherb by mountain settlers, giving rise to the common name. In spring, leafless stalks rise above the rosette bearing loose, airy clusters of small, white, five-petaled flowers. Unlike most garden perennials it cannot be grown in merely 'moist' soil -- it needs the equivalent of its native habitat, with roots perpetually bathed in cool, oxygenated running or seeping water, making it best suited to the edge of a garden stream, spring box, or continuously dripping rock wall. Good companions in such a setting include Chelone, Boykinia, and native ferns that share the same wet, cool microhabitat.

planting.note: Plant small divided mats in spring or fall into a continuously moist, cool, humus-rich seep or streambank site in partial shade; this high-elevation bluet spreads slowly and is best propagated by dividing established mats rather than relying on seed.

directions: Michaux's bluet is a high-elevation Southern Appalachian relative of the familiar lawn bluet, forming a dense, moss-like creeping mat of tiny, rounded, opposite leaves on wiry stems that roots as it spreads along wet rock faces, seep margins, and streambanks above roughly 3,000 feet. In late spring and summer it produces a steady scatter of small four-lobed flowers in a distinctive pale blue-violet, held just above the foliage on short pedicels. It requires the same continuously saturated, cool, humus-thin conditions as its native seep habitat and struggles in ordinary garden soil or summer heat, making it best suited to a shaded rock garden edge or bog garden with reliable year-round moisture. Because seed set is sparse outside its native seep habitat, division of established mats in spring or fall is the most reliable way to increase stock.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-propagated stock in fall into a thin, humus-poor, constantly seep-moistened rocky substrate in dappled shade, mimicking a cove-forest cliff face; source only from nurseries that propagate their own material, as this is an uncommon, narrow-range plant in the trade.

directions: Carey's saxifrage is a Blue Ridge escarpment endemic restricted to wet, mossy, seepage rock faces and cliff bases within cove-forest gorges along the North Carolina-South Carolina-Georgia-Tennessee border region. It forms a rosette of broad, spoon-shaped leaves from which rises a loose, airy panicle of small white flowers, the petals often flecked with purple-red spots near the base, opening in mid-spring. It is closely related to and sometimes confused in the trade with the more widespread Michaux's saxifrage, but Carey's saxifrage is restricted to a much narrower range and a more specialized rock-seepage habitat. In cultivation it needs a cool, humus-thin, constantly moist rocky substrate such as a dripping tufa wall or shaded rock garden seep, and should be treated as an uncommon specialty plant best sourced from nurseries propagating their own stock rather than wild-collected material.
